blocks.label: Pre-mid vs post-mid
blocks.text: Pre-mid = everything up to **information gain in decision trees**. Everything after that, including decision-tree overfitting, kNN and LWR, is post-mid. Across all four papers (160 marks) the split is **15% / 85%**.

blocks.label: How to use this paper
blocks.text: Open **Worked problems** and try each question on paper before revealing the steps.

worked.title: Q1 · Lasso or ensemble? (3 marks)

problem.text: Predict default risk (0–1). 60,000 samples, 500 features, only 10–15 truly matter, many correlated. Regulators require an auditable model with explainable feature contributions. Lasso RMSE 0.081; Random Forest / Gradient Boosting RMSE 0.062. (a) Which model? (b) Two disadvantages of the ensemble here.

steps.label: (a) Choose Lasso
steps.text: **Lasso (L1) regression**: it sets irrelevant coefficients exactly to zero, which suits "only 10–15 features matter". Its single linear equation is auditable and each coefficient shows a feature's contribution.

steps.label: (b) Disadvantage 1
steps.text: **Low interpretability**: hundreds of trees, no single equation, so it is hard to trace why a client got a score.

steps.label: (b) Disadvantage 2
steps.text: **Poor auditability / regulatory risk**: hard to justify decisions to the regulator or check fairness rules. Feature importances are approximate, not exact contributions.

worked.answer: Lasso; the ensemble is hard to interpret and hard to audit.

worked.title: Q2 · Weighted kNN with mixed attributes (6 marks)

problem.text: Training: A0 (35, 40k, Salaried, Tier-3, R2), A1 (45, 70k, Salaried, Tier-2, R2), A2 (30, 38k, Self-Emp, Tier-3, R1), A3 (50, 90k, Salaried, Tier-1, R2), A4 (28, 42k, Self-Emp, Tier-2, R1). Query Q = (32, 41k, Self-Emp, Tier-3). Weight = 1/d², all points used. (a) Distance, scores and class. (b) Why does R1 win with fewer samples? (c) Redo with City Tier as nominal.

steps.label: Distance
steps.text: Mixed numeric, nominal and ordinal attributes ⇒ **Gower distance**: the average of per-attribute distances, each in [0,1].

steps.label: Per attribute
steps.text: Age: |Δ|/22 (range 28–50). Spend: |Δ|/52k (range 38k–90k). Employment: 0 if same, else 1. City Tier (ordinal, 3 levels): |rank difference|/2.

steps.label: (b)
steps.text: Weighting uses similarity, not counts. A2 is extremely close (d ≈ 0.037), and 1/d² turns that into a huge weight that outvotes all three R2 points.

steps.label: (c) Nominal tier
steps.text: Tier mismatch now costs 1 instead of 0.5. A4: d = 0.3003, weight 11.09. A1: d = 0.7872, weight 1.61. Others unchanged.

worked.answer: Gower distance; R1 (757.12 vs 15.39); still R1 with nominal tier, R1 score lower by 21.47.

worked.title: Q3 · AdaBoost at iteration 3 (8 marks)

problem.text: Weights 0.1, 0.3, 0.15, 0.45; true labels +1, +1, −1, −1; h₃ predicts +1, −1, −1, −1. (a) Misclassified samples. (b) ε₃. (c) α₃ = ½ ln((1−ε)/ε). (d) Which sample has the highest weight, and what does that say? (e) One advantage and one disadvantage of AdaBoost vs a single tree.

steps.label: (a)
steps.text: Only **sample 2** (true +1, predicted −1).

steps.label: (d)
steps.text: **Sample 4** (0.45). It was probably misclassified in earlier rounds, so its weight kept growing. AdaBoost deliberately focuses later learners on the hard examples.

steps.label: (e)
steps.text: Advantage: higher accuracy, because many weak learners together reduce bias. Disadvantage: **sensitive to noise and outliers**, since it keeps raising the weight of points that may just be mislabelled, which can lead to overfitting.

worked.answer: Sample 2; ε₃ = 0.3; α₃ ≈ 0.424; sample 4 shows the focus on hard examples.

worked.title: Q5 · SVM for loan default (8 marks)

problem.text: Model A: linear SVM, C = 0.1, 85% train / 84% test. Model B: polynomial kernel, C = 100, degree 6, 98% train / 72% test. (a) Which overfits? What do C and degree do? What does this say about separability? (b) w = (0.5, −0.3), b = 0.2, x = (2, 1): compute f(x) and classify. (c) Geometric margin, and what a larger margin means. (d) Why soft margin?

steps.label: (a) Overfitting
steps.text: **Model B**: 98% train vs 72% test means it memorised the training data.

steps.label: (a) C and degree
steps.text: **C** is the penalty for margin violations. A large C (100) forces almost every training point to be classified correctly, including noise, so the boundary becomes complicated. **Degree** sets how wiggly the polynomial boundary can be, and degree 6 is very flexible.

steps.label: (a) Separability
steps.text: Model A's close train/test scores suggest the data is roughly **linearly separable with some overlap**. Model B's extra flexibility only fits noise.

steps.label: (c)
steps.text: ‖w‖ = √(0.25 + 0.09) = √0.34 ≈ 0.583. Geometric margin = 1/‖w‖ ≈ **1.715**, the distance from the boundary to each margin line. Full margin width = 2/‖w‖ ≈ 3.43. State which one you use. A larger margin means more confident predictions and better generalisation.

steps.label: (d)
steps.text: Loan data overlaps: some defaulters look like non-defaulters. A hard margin may have no solution. A **soft margin** allows a few violations (slack ξᵢ) to keep a wide, stable boundary.

worked.answer: Model B overfits; f(x) = 0.9 ⇒ default; margin 1/‖w‖ ≈ 1.715 (width 2/‖w‖ ≈ 3.43); soft margin handles overlap.

problem.text: Points A(1,2), B(2,1), C(2,3), D(6,5), E(7,6), F(8,5). (a) One K-means cycle from centres (1,2) and (8,5). (b) One difference between K-means assignments and GMM responsibilities, using a specific point. (c) When would GMM cluster this data better?

steps.label: (a) Assign
steps.text: A, B, C are nearest (1,2); D, E, F are nearest (8,5).

steps.label: (b)
steps.text: K-means gives **hard** assignments: C(2,3) belongs 100% to cluster 1. GMM gives **soft responsibilities**: C gets a probability for each component, mostly cluster 1 but with a small non-zero share for cluster 2.

steps.label: (c)
steps.text: When clusters are **elliptical, of different spread, or overlapping**: GMM models each cluster's covariance and the uncertainty of assignment, while K-means assumes round clusters of equal size.

worked.title: Q7 · Linear, logistic, tree (3 marks)

problem.text: Same two features. A: linear regression with a threshold; B: logistic regression; C: depth-3 tree. A gives values outside [0,1]; B saturates near 0/1; C flips class for small changes in x₂. (a) Why can A leave [0,1] but B cannot? (b) Which overfits most on small data? (c) Which changes most abruptly, and why is that bad?

steps.label: (a)
steps.text: A outputs wᵀx + b, which is **unbounded**. B passes the same score through the **sigmoid**, which always lands in (0,1).

steps.label: (b)
steps.text: The **decision tree**: its boundary is made of flexible axis-aligned splits (piecewise constant) that can chase noise. Linear and logistic models draw one global straight boundary, a stronger bias that generalises better on little data.

steps.label: (c)
steps.text: The **decision tree**: a tiny change can cross a split threshold and flip the class. Such jumps are unstable and hard to justify, which hurts fairness and trust in high-stakes decisions.

worked.answer: Sigmoid bounds B; the tree overfits most and changes most abruptly.
